todays_goal: Start with a rigorous Math Accuracy Clinic, repair negative-possession French, advance refraction into lenses and Greek history into the causes of the Peloponnesian War, strengthen close reading and analytical writing, and protect a long practical vibe-coding Builder Lab.

lessons.subject: mathematics
lessons.lesson_title: Accuracy Clinic: Percent mastery and execution
lessons.previous_learning: Day 13 showed strong conceptual understanding of percent but inconsistent execution: required estimates and methods were omitted, percent notation and multi-part answers were sometimes incomplete, one unknown-whole problem was incorrect, and the mastery gate was below the 90% standard.
lessons.course_context: Today's designated cumulative-review subject. The target is reliable execution: read, label, estimate, solve, verify, complete.
learning_objectives: Solve find-the-part, find-the-percent, and find-the-whole problems accurately.
Use benchmark estimates before exact work.
Complete every requested part, unit, method, and check.
Analyze and repair percent errors.
lessons.why_it_matters: Highly selective academic settings expect correct reasoning, reliable arithmetic, complete responses, and independent checking rather than approximate understanding alone.

vocabulary.definition: the amount being compared with the whole
the complete amount
a rate per 100
a familiar value used for a quick estimate
a second check that supports accuracy

lessons.written_instruction: Accuracy Protocol: READ the exact task; LABEL part, percent, whole, and unknown; ESTIMATE with a benchmark; SOLVE with visible arithmetic; VERIFY the size/result; COMPLETE every requested part, unit, label, explanation, and second output. A correct number can still be an incomplete response.

worked_examples.title: Find the part - deeply annotated
worked_examples.explanation: Whole=350, percent=0.18, part unknown. Estimate with 20%: 70. Compute 0.18 x 350 = 63. Since 63 is slightly below 70, the answer is reasonable.

worked_examples.title: Find the percent - deeply annotated
worked_examples.explanation: Part=42, whole=120, percent unknown. Estimate a little above one-third. Compute 42/120=0.35, then convert to 35%. Reverse check: 0.35 x 120 = 42.

worked_examples.title: Find the whole - deeply annotated
worked_examples.explanation: Part=56, percent=0.40, whole unknown. Estimate whole >112. Compute 56/0.40=140. Check: 40% of 140=56.

worked_examples.title: Multi-part discount - deeply annotated
worked_examples.problem: A $150 item is discounted 18%. Find discount AND sale price.
worked_examples.explanation: First find discount 0.18 x 150 = 27, then subtract 150-27=123. Check against a 20% benchmark and verify 27+123=150.

guided_practice.prompt: Accuracy warm-up: solve 0.18x300, 0.42x150, 0.75x84, 32/80 to percent, 27/120 to percent, 84/0.35, 0.25x96 then subtract, and 45/0.30. No calculator; use large-grid workspace.

independent_practice.prompt: Find 24% of 275. Estimate with 25% first.
Find 38% of 250. Show decimal multiplication.
54 is what percent of 120? Include the percent symbol and a reverse check.
72 is 30% of what whole? Check by finding 30% of your answer.
A $128 pair of shoes is discounted 25%. Find BOTH discount and sale price.
ERROR ANALYSIS: A student says 35% of 160 = 560. Explain why unreasonable and repair.

exit_ticket.prompt: A $180 item is discounted 15%. Find BOTH discount and sale price.

lessons.voice_prompt: Be demanding but calm and concise. Never call an incomplete response correct. If the number is right but a required method, unit, second answer, estimate, or check is missing, say the number is right but the response is incomplete. Never give the assigned final answer. Identify the first error or missing requirement only, give one concise cue, and require a retry.
lessons.teacher_notes: Do not advance the percent unit until 90% mastery with complete multi-part responses.

lessons.subject: french
lessons.previous_learning: Day 13 showed être/avoir selection is substantially secure but negative possession remained incorrect because un/une/des was not consistently changed to de and elision was inconsistent.
lessons.course_context: Isolate the one remaining grammar gap and make it automatic before adding new grammar.
learning_objectives: Produce ne/n'...pas de in negative possession.
Use correct avoir conjugation and elision.
Reach at least 9/10 transformations orally and in writing.
lessons.why_it_matters: Automatic high-frequency grammar supports accurate speaking and frees attention for richer French communication.

vocabulary.definition: ne/n' + avoir + pas + de + noun
dropping a vowel before another vowel sound, as in ne becoming n'

lessons.written_instruction: Positive possession uses avoir. In most negative possession sentences, place ne/n' and pas around avoir and change un/une/des to de. Example: J'ai un livre -> Je n'ai pas de livre.

worked_examples.title: Plural negative possession
worked_examples.explanation: Des becomes de and ne elides to n' before a.

independent_practice.prompt: J'ai un stylo -> negative
Elle a des cahiers -> negative
Nous avons une voiture -> negative
Ils ont des devoirs -> negative
Tu as un chien -> negative
J'ai une calculatrice -> negative
Nous avons des livres -> negative
Vous avez une question -> negative

exit_ticket.prompt: Oral/written mastery: at least 9/10 negative-possession transformations correct.
exit_ticket.answer: At least nine grammatically correct ne/n'...pas de possession sentences.

lessons.voice_prompt: Oral first. Do not reteach être/avoir unless the meaning choice is wrong. If Atticus uses un, une, or des after pas, say only: Check the noun phrase after pas. Require the corrected full sentence; do not supply it.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.previous_learning: Day 13 showed Atticus understands the bent-pencil refraction phenomenon and produced a useful air-water-eye ray model, but his written mechanism was too vague and the coin-reveal investigation was incomplete.
lessons.course_context: Advance by applying refraction to curved transparent surfaces and convex lenses while continuing to require mechanism-level explanations.
learning_objectives: Define a lens as a refracting transparent object with curved surfaces.
Explain how a convex lens redirects parallel rays.
Explain magnification as a changed light path and apparent image.
Connect lens behavior to prior refraction learning.
lessons.why_it_matters: Lenses connect refraction to cameras, eyes, microscopes, telescopes, and other technologies.

vocabulary.definition: a transparent object with curved surfaces that refracts light
a lens thicker in the middle that can bend parallel rays toward one another
the region where refracted rays meet or become concentrated
a point where parallel rays come together in a simple model

lessons.written_instruction: A lens applies refraction at curved boundaries. Different rays meet the surface at different angles, so their directions change differently. A convex lens can bend parallel rays toward one another and can create an enlarged apparent image in the correct viewing position.

worked_examples.title: Convex lens
worked_examples.problem: Parallel rays enter a convex lens.
worked_examples.solution: Rays bend toward one another after leaving the lens.
worked_examples.explanation: Curved air-glass and glass-air boundaries refract rays at different angles.

worked_examples.title: Magnifier
worked_examples.problem: Why can a magnifying glass make text look larger?
worked_examples.solution: The lens changes ray directions before they reach the eye.
worked_examples.explanation: The light path changes; the printed letters do not physically enlarge.

independent_practice.prompt: What is a lens, and what property of light makes it useful?
Why do rays entering near a convex lens edge change direction differently from a central ray?
Draw three parallel rays entering a convex lens and bending toward one another. Label lens and focal region.
Explain why a magnifying glass can make an object appear larger although the object has not changed size.
How is a lens an application of refraction rather than a completely new phenomenon?

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain in two sentences how a convex lens changes light-ray paths.
exit_ticket.answer: Curved lens boundaries refract rays by different amounts; a convex lens can bend parallel rays toward one another.

exit_ticket.prompt: Why is saying the lens makes things bigger incomplete scientifically?
exit_ticket.answer: The object does not change size; the lens changes ray directions and the apparent image.

lessons.voice_prompt: Require mechanism, not labels. Because of refraction is incomplete. Ask what medium changes, where the boundary is, how ray direction changes, and what happens to rays after the lens. Do not draw assigned diagrams.
lessons.teacher_notes: Keep refraction alive through retrieval while advancing to lenses.

lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.previous_learning: Day 13 history was strong: Atticus understood the Delian League, Athenian control of fleet and treasury, coercion of members, and the cause chain toward tension with Sparta.
lessons.course_context: Advance from growth of Athenian power to a multi-cause explanation of why rivalry became war.
learning_objectives: Explain multiple long-term causes of the Peloponnesian War.
Explain how alliance systems can escalate local disputes.
Distinguish a multi-cause explanation from a simplistic one-cause claim.
Defend a judgment about the most important cause using evidence.
lessons.why_it_matters: Historical explanation requires weighing interacting causes rather than memorizing isolated events.

vocabulary.definition: a long conflict between Athens and its allies and Sparta and its allies
competition between groups seeking power or advantage
a network of agreements that can pull multiple states into a conflict
dominant influence or leadership over other states
a process in which conflict becomes more intense

lessons.written_instruction: After the Persian Wars, Athenian naval power and influence expanded through the Delian League. Sparta remained the strongest land power. Fear of Athenian growth, competing interests, alliance commitments, and shorter-term disputes combined to make compromise harder. The war cannot be explained by one cause alone.

independent_practice.prompt: What long-term change after the Persian Wars increased Athenian power?
Why could Athenian growth create fear in Sparta and its allies?
How could alliance systems turn a smaller dispute into a larger war?
Why is Athens and Sparta were different an incomplete explanation for the war?
Build a four-link cause chain from Athenian growth to war.
Which cause was most important: power, fear, economic interests, or alliances? Defend with evidence.

exit_ticket.prompt: In 5 sentences, explain why historians should avoid a one-cause explanation for the Peloponnesian War. Use at least two causes.
exit_ticket.answer: A full response connects multiple factors such as Athenian growth, Spartan fear and security concerns, competing interests, and alliance systems.

lessons.voice_prompt: Require multi-cause reasoning. If Atticus gives only one cause, ask what other pressure made the situation more dangerous. Distinguish long-term causes from immediate disputes. Do not supply the final explanation.
lessons.teacher_notes: History is strong; advance rigor through causal analysis.

lessons.subject: literature
lessons.lesson_title: The Quiet Prototype: inference, diction, and evidence significance
lessons.previous_learning: Day 13 literature was strong: Atticus identified motivation, turning point, theme, evidence significance, and diction. Writing still needs greater precision and completeness.
lessons.course_context: Increase reading difficulty and integrate a short analytical paragraph so close reading transfers into writing.
learning_objectives: Infer motivation from exact evidence.
Explain how diction shapes meaning.
Support a universal theme with evidence and significance.
Write a concise analytical paragraph using two exact details.
lessons.why_it_matters: Selective-school-level reading requires not only comprehension but precise interpretation and evidence-based writing.

vocabulary.definition: an author's choice of words
the feeling or association a word carries
a conclusion based on evidence and reasoning
why a character chooses an action
a universal message developed by a text
what a detail proves or reveals

lessons.written_instruction: Read The Quiet Prototype closely. Do not answer a significance question with plot summary. After citing a detail, explain what the detail proves or reveals about motivation, problem solving, or theme.

independent_practice.prompt: What problem is hidden by the prototype's flashy features at the beginning?
Why does Mara unplug the buzzer? State her motivation, not just the action.
What does the single word Listening reveal about how Mara approaches the problem?
Why is the faint scrape an important piece of evidence?
Explain the significance of the final line Only if we finish early.
Write one universal theme statement.
Give two pieces of evidence for the theme and explain the significance of each.
Write a 3-sentence objective summary.
ANALYTICAL WRITING: In 6-8 sentences, explain why removing the buzzer was a productive decision. Use two exact details and explain why each matters.

exit_ticket.prompt: Choose one word or short phrase whose diction matters. Explain what the wording suggests beyond the literal event.
exit_ticket.answer: A strong response identifies a specific word or phrase and explains its connotation or interpretive effect.

lessons.voice_prompt: Do not accept plot summary when the question asks for significance. Ask what the detail proves or reveals. Require precise evidence. For the analytical paragraph, do not dictate sentences; identify only one issue at a time and require revision.
lessons.teacher_notes: Advance reading difficulty while keeping writing precision explicit.

lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.unit_title: Creative Technology and AI Builder Lab
lessons.previous_learning: Friday's Builder Lab was not attempted. The curriculum now reflects Atticus's real workflow: he vibe codes with an AI coding agent and is not expected to use an IDE or know syntax.
lessons.course_context: Protected 75-minute practical build focused on specification, prompting, testing, behavioral debugging, creative product judgment, iteration, and shipping.
learning_objectives: Describe a product clearly in natural language.
Write observable acceptance criteria.
Direct an AI coding agent through focused iterations.
Playtest adaptive behavior and write a behavioral bug report.
Ship a working creative upgrade.
lessons.why_it_matters: Future technical leverage comes from turning ideas into working systems, directing AI tools precisely, testing behavior, debugging, and exercising product judgment.

vocabulary.definition: a clear description of what a product should do
observable rules used to judge whether a feature works
one build-test-improve cycle
behavior that does not match the intended product
describing, fixing, and retesting a problem
information the product remembers, such as earlier kicks

lessons.written_instruction: Vibe-coding loop: IMAGINE -> SPECIFY -> BUILD with AI agent -> PLAY -> JUDGE -> ITERATE one focused change -> TEST -> SHIP. The Penalty Predictor starts as a random goalkeeper, then is upgraded through natural-language requests to remember LEFT/CENTER/RIGHT history, display a Keeper Brain, adapt to player tendencies while retaining randomness, and add one creative feature.

guided_practice.prompt: Define the version-1 game vibe and write five acceptance criteria before asking the AI coding agent to build.

independent_practice.prompt: Write the natural-language request for version 1 of the Penalty Predictor.
Play at least eight kicks and record one strong feature and one weak or broken experience.
Write a focused request to add player-history memory, a visible Keeper Brain, and adaptive goalkeeper behavior with some randomness.
Playtest: repeat one direction, change strategy, then try to fool the keeper.
Write one behavioral bug report using EXPECTED -> ACTUAL -> STEPS TO REPRODUCE -> TEST AFTER FIX.
Choose and ship one creative upgrade: streak mode, commentator, mind-read meter, difficulty modes, fakeout mechanic, player or club customization, or your own idea.

exit_ticket.prompt: Show the working product and explain in plain language how the goalkeeper becomes more informed after several kicks.
exit_ticket.answer: The game remembers prior choices, detects a tendency, and changes goalkeeper behavior while keeping some unpredictability.

materials: AI coding agent with live preview
lessons.voice_prompt: Act as a product coach, not a coding lecturer. Do not require an IDE, manual code editing, or syntax knowledge. If Atticus asks what to prompt next, first ask what behavior he wants changed, then help make that request precise with acceptance criteria. Encourage one focused change at a time followed by playtesting. Help write behavioral bug reports. Do not take over the entire build.
lessons.teacher_notes: Assess specification quality, acceptance criteria, focused prompting, playtesting, behavioral debugging, creative judgment, and whether a working product is shipped; do not grade syntax.
